economy.summary: She proposes SME credit and tax holidays, farming clusters and local processing of raw materials; none is costed.
economy.analysis:
Okwori's economic proposals come from two sources: the party spokesperson at her June 2026 unveiling and her own September 2026 Blueprint interview. The spokesperson described a 'deliberate' shift towards processing natural resources at home and exporting finished goods instead of raw materials, together with basic infrastructure to support growth. In the interview she described an 'NDP Prosperity Plan': low-interest loans, three-year tax holidays and digital market access for small businesses; mechanised farming clusters with storage and guaranteed buyers for farmers; and decentralised solar and gas power for states and industrial hubs.

The proposals name instruments but give no estimate of cost, of revenue forgone through tax holidays, or of who would provide the low-interest credit (the CBN, development banks or commercial lenders). Value-addition policies have been attempted under earlier administrations, and their results depended on power supply, foreign-exchange access and port efficiency. Most of those conditions sit outside presidential control, and the sources reviewed do not discuss them. No positions were found on the exchange rate, fuel subsidy, inflation or tariffs, which dominate current federal economic decisions. The proposals are therefore assessable only as stated intentions.
strengths: Names specific instruments (credit, tax holidays, farming clusters)
limitations: No positions on exchange rate, subsidy, inflation or trade policy

security.summary: Her 'Safe Nigeria Agenda' lists community policing, surveillance technology, welfare for personnel and youth programmes, without detail on funding or legal changes.
security.analysis:
In her Blueprint interview Okwori outlined an 'NDP Safe Nigeria Agenda' made up of community policing, intelligence and technology such as drones, support for local security structures, better welfare for security personnel, and jobs and skills programmes for young people at risk of recruitment into crime. The party's June 2026 unveiling statement did not address security.

Several of these elements interact with the constitution: the Nigeria Police Force is federal, so any community or state-level policing structure with coercive powers would likely require constitutional amendment through the National Assembly and state assemblies, which she does not address. Drone surveillance and welfare improvements carry recurring costs that are not estimated. She does not say how the plan would relate to the military's internal-security deployments or to existing state security outfits. She has no record of overseeing security agencies, so the category rests on proposals only. As with all candidates, actual outcomes would depend on state governments, community cooperation and regional conditions as well as federal choices.
limitations: Constitutional route for community policing not addressed
unknowns: Command and legal structure of the proposed community policing
Cost of technology and welfare commitments

education.summary: She proposes allocating 15% of the national budget to education, upgrading 5,000 public schools in a first term and setting up vocational centres in every LGA.
education.analysis:
Education is one of the few areas where Okwori has stated numerical targets. Her 'Future Minds Initiative', described in the Blueprint interview, includes better pay, training and housing for teachers; vocational centres in every local government area; free coding and technical training; 15 per cent of the national budget for education; and upgrades to 5,000 public schools in the first term. The June 2026 unveiling statement also referred broadly to quality education and human-capital investment.

The targets are measurable, which allows later checking, but the interview gives no costing, no comparison with the current federal allocation, and no account of how a federal government would upgrade schools that states and local governments mostly own and run. Basic education is largely a state and local responsibility, with federal support through UBEC transfers that require state counterpart funds. A higher federal education share would require either new revenue or cuts elsewhere, and it would need National Assembly approval through appropriation. None of these trade-offs is discussed in the sources.
strengths: Measurable targets (15% budget share, 5,000 schools, vocational centre per LGA)
limitations: Federal–state division of responsibility not addressed
unknowns: Baseline federal education share she is comparing against

healthcare.summary: Only a general commitment to 'accessible, affordable healthcare for all' was found.
healthcare.analysis: The party spokesperson listed accessible and affordable healthcare among her priorities at the June 2026 unveiling. No proposals on health insurance, financing, primary healthcare or tertiary hospitals were found.
missing: Position on national health insurance and primary healthcare funding

infrastructure.summary: Only a general reference to 'basic infrastructure that supports economic growth and jobs' was found.
infrastructure.analysis: No named projects, sector priorities (roads, rail, ports, housing) or financing approaches were found beyond the spokesperson's general statement.

power.summary: She proposes decentralised solar and gas power for states and industrial hubs, without further detail.
power.analysis: The Blueprint interview mentions decentralised solar and gas power for states and industrial hubs as part of the Prosperity Plan. No capacity targets, costs, or positions on the national grid, tariffs or distribution companies were found.
missing: Position on grid, tariffs and DisCos

jobs.summary: She has stated a target of 10 million jobs in four years tied to small-business support, without a method for counting or reaching it.
jobs.analysis: The 10 million jobs target appears in the Blueprint interview as an outcome of SME credit, tax holidays and digital market access, alongside youth innovation hubs in every state. The interview gives no baseline, sector breakdown or measurement method.
missing: Baseline and measurement method for the jobs target
Sector breakdown and cost per job

finance.summary: She proposes eliminating waste, an open budget portal and project tracking, but has no stated position on debt or revenue.
finance.analysis: The party spokesperson spoke of eliminating waste and leakages across government; Okwori's interview adds an open budget portal, project tracking and quarterly published results. No position was found on borrowing, debt service, revenue mobilisation or how tax holidays would be offset.
missing: Revenue plan and fiscal offsets for proposed tax holidays

leadership.summary: She founded the NDP and chairs it by court order; she proposes performance contracts and term limits, but has no public-office record.
leadership.analysis: Okwori led the NDP's registration effort, including a successful suit against INEC, and is its National Chairman by court order. She also became its presidential candidate, so she holds the party's top organisational and electoral roles at once. Her proposals include performance contracts for office holders with quarterly published results, town-hall consultations and a binding party code of conduct. No record of running a public institution was found.
missing: Evidence of how she has run teams or budgets
Composition of her campaign and policy team

integrity.summary: No court case, investigation or allegation against her was found; this reflects limited coverage, not a confirmed clean record.
integrity.analysis: The only court matter found is the NDP registration suit, in which she was a plaintiff and won. OurNigeria reports no case against her. No asset declaration was found.

experience.summary: No public office held. Her record consists of grassroots mobilisation, PDP-era activism, and founding and litigating the NDP into registration.
experience.analysis:
Okwori has not held elected or appointed public office. INEC lists her qualifications as FSLC, SSCE and an HND in Accountancy; no institution or occupation was found. OurNigeria and the Advocate report that she is Idoma, from Adoka in Benue State, and founded Ward2Ward, a ward-level mobilisation group. As its national coordinator in October 2014 she campaigned for President Goodluck Jonathan's 2015 re-election. She was an earlier PDP member, and in April 2024 a youth group backed her for PDP National Women Leader, though no vote on that post was found.

Her most documented achievement is organisational and legal. After INEC declined to register the NDP in December 2025, she and three other promoters sued, and the Federal High Court, Abuja, ordered registration on 16 February 2026 (suit FHC/ABJ/CS/2796/2025, as reported). INEC's party page lists her as National Chairman by court order. The party named her its consensus candidate after primaries on 29 May 2026 but announced this on 1 June, after INEC's 30 May deadline, which BusinessDay reported raised eligibility questions. She nonetheless appears on INEC's final list, with Chukwuemeka Uchenna Anthony as her running mate.
strengths: Built and registered a national party through litigation
limitations: No public-office or large-budget management record
Education institutions and occupation not documented

vision.summary: She presents the NDP as an inclusive, accountability-focused alternative built on 'true federalism', local value addition and women's and youth participation.
vision.analysis:
Okwori's stated vision combines governance reform with economic and social inclusion. At the June 2026 unveiling, the party spokesperson described an 'inclusive administration' that would bring women and youth into decision-making, 'true federalism' with fairness and accountability across the three tiers of government, and an end to waste and leakages. In her own words she framed her candidacy around the need for women in national leadership: 'I will not fail you; I will not fail my country'.

In the September Blueprint interview she described the NDP's founding principles as integrity, accountability, service, inclusion and nation-building. She proposed screening candidates on 'capacity and character rather than money', a minimum of 40 per cent women in party executives and candidate lists, a 35 per cent youth quota in party structures, and a Women's Leadership Fund. Some of these are commitments about how she runs her party, not government policy, and can be checked against the NDP's own lists. 'True federalism' is not defined in the sources, so its implications for revenue sharing, policing or resource control are unknown. A full manifesto was promised in June 2026 but was not found.
strengths: Stated principles are paired with some checkable party commitments (40% women, 35% youth quota)
unknowns: Meaning of 'true federalism' in policy terms
Whether NDP candidate lists meet the 40% women target

foreign.analysis: No positions on ECOWAS, trade agreements, the diaspora or security cooperation were found. The value-addition and export proposal touches trade but is framed domestically.

humanImpact.summary: She proposes social support for the elderly and retirees and inclusion of women and youth; no programme detail was found.
humanImpact.analysis: The party spokesperson listed social support for the elderly and retirees. Her interview adds youth innovation hubs and a Women's Leadership Fund. No eligibility rules, scale or costs were given, and no record of past welfare programmes she ran was found.
missing: Design and cost of the elderly and retiree support
Scale and funding of the Women's Leadership Fund

promises.summary: Her commitments include several measurable targets (10 million jobs, 15% of the budget to education, 5,000 schools), but none is costed or scheduled beyond 'four years' or 'first term'.
promises.analysis:
Across the June 2026 unveiling and the September 2026 interview, Okwori's campaign made more quantified commitments than most lesser-known candidates: 10 million jobs in four years, a 15 per cent budget share for education, 5,000 upgraded public schools in a first term, vocational centres in every LGA, a youth innovation hub in every state, and a 40 per cent women's representation floor in the party. Other commitments are qualitative, such as decentralised power, community policing, an open budget portal and mandatory asset declarations.

The quantified targets make later accountability possible, but none is accompanied by a cost estimate, a funding source, a sequencing plan or a discussion of trade-offs. For example, the tax holidays and higher education spending pull the budget in opposite directions without any stated offset. Several promises, including budget shares and asset-declaration rules, need National Assembly action. The NDP promised a full manifesto 'soon' in June 2026, and none was found by late November 2026, so these commitments come only from press statements and one interview. They are listed individually under plans.
limitations: Commitments come from press statements, not a published manifesto
unknowns: Whether a manifesto has been published
Costing of the commitments as a package

record.title: Won suit compelling INEC to register the NDP
record.label: FACT
record.description: As lead plaintiff with three other promoters (suit FHC/ABJ/CS/2796/2025, as reported), she obtained a Federal High Court order directing INEC to register the NDP. INEC's party page records her chairmanship 'by court order'. This is a party-building outcome, not a record in public office.
